html:
Ur was one of the great Sumerian city-states of southern Mesopotamia, near the mouth of the Euphrates, in what is now southern Iraq. People lived there from about 3800 BCE, and it was abandoned around 500 BCE. On this map it stands for southern Mesopotamia in 3000 and 2000 BCE.

Around 2600 BCE its rulers were buried in the Royal Cemetery with gold, lyres, the Royal Game of Ur board and, in some tombs, dozens of attendants who died with them. After the fall of the Akkadian Empire, Ur-Nammu made Ur the capital of the Third Dynasty of Ur around 2100 BCE. He built the Great Ziggurat and issued the Code of Ur-Nammu, the oldest law code known. His son Shulgi ran a vast bureaucracy.

Around 2004 BCE the Elamites sacked Ur, a disaster mourned in the Lament for Ur. The city lived on as a religious centre for the moon god Nanna. The Bible names "Ur of the Chaldees" as the home of Abraham. Leonard Woolley excavated it in the 1920s and 1930s.
